## Question

Over a long horizon, which integrator reaches a given energy accuracy on a
Kepler orbit for less work: an adaptive Dormand-Prince 5(4) Runge-Kutta
method or the fixed-step Stormer-Verlet method? The operating point is an
orbit of eccentricity 0.5{claim:eccentricity}, a horizon of
1000{claim:norbits} orbits, and a budget of 1e-6{claim:target} on the
largest relative energy error seen at any step. The quantity of interest is
the cost ratio: Verlet force evaluations over DP5(4) right-hand-side
evaluations, each at its cheapest setting that meets the budget. A factor
of two is accurate enough to answer the question, since the answer is
which method to use.

## Scales and estimate

With GM = 1 and semi-major axis a = 1 the period is 2 pi and the energy is
-1/2, so one orbit is the natural unit of time and the relative energy
error needs no scale of its own. Before any long run: Verlet's energy error
is bounded and scales as h^2, and at about 100 steps per orbit an orbit of
this eccentricity keeps its energy to about 1e-2 near perihelion, so 1e-6
needs about 100 times more steps per orbit. My estimate was
10000{estimate:verlet_nper} steps per orbit.

## Model and assumptions

The two-body problem with the Sun fixed: q'' = -q/|q|^3, a planar orbit,
started at perihelion. No other bodies, no relativity. Accuracy is judged by
a proxy, the largest relative energy error over the horizon; the proxy is
checked against the true orbit under Validation. Cost is counted in
right-hand-side (force) evaluations, not seconds, so it does not depend on
the machine.

## Method choice

The cheapest DP5(4) setting that meets the budget is
rtol = atol = 3.16e-9{claim:tol_dp54}, with an energy error of
7.9e-7{claim:err_dp54} for 506498{claim:nf_dp54} evaluations. The
cheapest Verlet setting is 10372{claim:nper_verlet} steps per orbit, with
an energy error of 9.97e-7{claim:err_verlet} for
10372001{claim:nf_verlet} force evaluations. I choose
dp54{claim:choice}.

The cost ratio is 20.5{claim:cost_ratio}: Verlet needs about twenty times
the work. The search grids bound it between 20.3{claim:cost_ratio_lo} and
23.0{claim:cost_ratio_hi} (the cost of the setting that just failed and
the one that passed, for each method), well inside the factor of two the
question needs.

## Verification

The code is right on problems with known answers. A 6x6 nilpotent linear
system, whose solution is a polynomial of degree 5 in t, is solved by seven
fixed DP5 steps with error 2.7e-15{claim:exact_linear_err}, rounding
error only.

On one period of the orbit with fixed steps, the fitted order of DP5 is
5.18{claim:conv_order} for step sizes from 3.93e-3{claim:conv_fit_hmin}
to 3.14e-2{claim:conv_fit_hmax}.

The fitted order of Verlet is 2.000{claim:verlet_order} for step sizes
from 1.96e-3{claim:verlet_fit_hmin} to 1.57e-2{claim:verlet_fit_hmax}.
The adaptive solver's error over one period is proportional to the
tolerance: the fitted slope is 1.03{claim:tol_slope} for tolerances from
1e-5 to 1e-10.

## Validation

The proxy has to answer the real question, where the planet is. At the
end of the horizon the position error against the exact orbit (Kepler's
equation) is 0.0060{claim:pos_err_dp54} for DP5(4) and
0.0164{claim:pos_err_verlet} for Verlet, in units of the semi-major axis,
at the settings chosen above. Both methods meet the energy budget with
position errors of the same order, so the energy proxy does not favour
one method on position accuracy; Verlet's error is mostly phase (a lag
along the orbit), which energy does not see.

## Uncertainty and sensitivity

The energy error grows as k to the power 0.99{claim:drift_exp_dp54} for
DP5(4) and 4.8e-7{claim:drift_exp_verlet} for Verlet, fitted over
40{claim:drift_fit_kmin} to 1280{claim:drift_fit_kmax} orbits: linear
drift for Runge-Kutta, bounded error for the symplectic method. The first
orbits carry a transient and were left out of the fit. The ratio therefore
depends on the horizon: DP5(4)'s advantage shrinks as the horizon grows,
and at some much longer horizon Verlet wins. This study did not find that
horizon.

The DP5(4) setting has its own uncertainty: over 1000 orbits the energy
error is not monotone in the tolerance (1e-9 misses the budget that the
looser 3.16e-9 meets), so the cheapest tolerance is the first pass of a
search from loose to tight on a stated grid, here quarter decades from
1e-6. A finer grid could find a cheaper pass; the bounds on the cost ratio
above are for this grid.

The perturbed assumption: at eccentricity 0.6{claim:robust_e} the cost
ratio is 19.4{claim:robust_cost_ratio}, the choice is still
dp54{claim:robust_choice}, so the conclusion holds{claim:robust_holds}.

## Claims and limits

At the operating point, DP5(4) reaches the energy budget for about a
twentieth of Verlet's work, and the fitted orders and the exact solution
say the code is right. This was tested for eccentricities from
0.5{claim:valid_e_min} to 0.6{claim:valid_e_max} and horizons up to
1000{claim:valid_norbits_max} orbits, and is claimed nowhere else: not
for more eccentric orbits, not for longer horizons where Verlet's bounded
error must eventually win, and not for cost in seconds, which also
depends on how cheap each force evaluation is.
